newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Kuwaiti seeks $30 million from Iraq for stolen art.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaiti seeks $30 million from Iraq for stolen art.

text.p: A Kuwaiti whose prestigious collection of Islamic art was stolen during Iraq's occupation of the emirate has filed a $30 million claim against Baghdad, the United Nations reparations fund disclosed on Thursday.
The U.N. Compensation Commission said that an Islamic art expert would assist its panel of neutral judges who are evaluating Jasim Homaizi's claim for damages.
Interpol and major auction houses have been alerted to watch for any trace of the 400 works, which include ceramics, paintings and other artefacts, some dating from the 4th century.
Private detectives are also on the trail and two people have been caught in Geneva and London allegedly trying to unload stolen pieces.
"The collection was considered to be one of the most prestigious and best-known in Islamic art circles," the U.N. statement said.

"Many of its most precious pieces ended up in Baghdad and Amman where dealers have tried to smuggle them out to Western cities," it added. "More than one clandestine seller has been apprehended and several pieces have been recovered."
Homaizi was the first of some 11,000 wealthy individuals from 60 countries to file for damages in excess of $100,000. Roughly half of these individuals are Kuwaitis.
"There are other significant claims for other types of art collections and jewellery. But this claim is unique," a U.N. source told Reuters.

The commission, set up by the Security Council to assess claims resulting from Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait and seven-month occupation, has received claims from individuals, corporations and governments worth more than $200 billion.

Claims filed by individuals who were either forced to flee Kuwait or Iraq or who suffered personal injury, loss of possessions or death of a close relative, will get priority over the corporate and governmental claims.

The fund -- which will receive 30 percent of the revenues generated by the limited Iraqi oil sales -- received a boost when Iraqi oil began to flow this week after a six-year hiatus. Under the oil-for-food accord, it will get $100 million a month.
Homaizi alerted Interpol and Scotland Yard to the theft of his artworks and has hired private detectives to follow up on "illicit transactions", according to the U.N. statement.
Major auction houses, including Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips have been warned that stolen pieces might be on the market, it added.
"The most prominent pieces in the collection appear in numerous art catalogues," the commission said.

One of the most beautiful pieces from Homaizi's collection, a 14th-century Iznik porcelain dish, was chosen by the Organising Committee of the Atlantic Olympics to represent Islamic art in an exhibit entitled "Rings" at the recent games.
